analysis.one_liner: Raises fines for failing to clean up oil and hazardous-substance spills and adds criminal penalties.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past a House subcommittee and died when the 101st Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Following a period of public concern over oil spills, this bill would have quintupled the fines against companies that fail to comply with federal cleanup rules for discharged oil and hazardous substances, from $5,000 per violation to up to $25,000 per day per violation. It would have let the EPA collect unpaid fines through the courts, add interest, fees, and a 20% quarterly nonpayment charge, force violators to fix problems through compliance orders, and impose criminal penalties for negligent, knowing, or knowingly false conduct. The bill was referred to committee and then to a subcommittee, where it stayed until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal communities, fishermen, tourism businesses, and water users who bear the damage when companies fail to clean up oil and hazardous-substance spills. Stronger, faster-enforced penalties give companies a bigger financial reason to follow cleanup regulations in the first place, so fewer spills go unremediated.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Coastal communities and people who use public waters

how_it_helps.text: Raises the civil penalty for failing to comply with regulations on removing discharged oil or hazardous substances from $5,000 per violation to up to $25,000 per day per violation, and lets the EPA Administrator sue to collect it.

Requires violators to pay interest, collection costs, attorneys' fees, and a nonpayment penalty equal to 20% of unpaid penalties for each quarter they go unpaid, and gives accused parties court review of penalty orders.

Requires the EPA to issue compliance orders telling violators to fix the problem within 60 days, allows orders to require environmental audits of the affected facility and similar facilities, and lets the EPA sue to enforce orders and to seek injunctions and penalties up to $25,000 per day.

Imposes criminal penalties, tied to existing Clean Water Act punishment levels, for negligent violations, knowing violations, knowing violations that put people in imminent danger of death or serious injury, and knowingly false statements in required filings.

Tells the courts and the agency to size penalties based on the risk of the violation and the economic benefit the violator gained from noncompliance, rather than the violator's good faith after getting caught.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that store, transport, or handle oil and hazardous substances, which would face fines up to five times higher, mandatory compliance orders and environmental audits, collection add-ons for nonpayment, and criminal exposure for serious or knowing violations. In practice, companies that complied with cleanup rules would pay nothing more.

drawbacks.text: The bill's penalty structure is severe: fines of up to $25,000 per day per violation, plus a 20% quarterly nonpayment penalty and attorneys' fees, could impose very large costs on businesses, including smaller operators, for regulatory violations even where no spill or environmental harm occurred.

The bill limits the procedures for the administrative penalty hearing and restricts judicial review, directing courts to uphold penalty orders unless there is no substantial evidence for the finding or the assessment was an abuse of discretion — a lighter check on the agency than full de novo review.

Enforcement penalties alone do not prevent spills; critics of penalty-focused approaches argue that compliance requirements, spill-prevention standards, and response capability matter more than the size of the fine after the fact.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits — a much stronger financial deterrent against failing to clean up oil and hazardous-substance discharges — fall on companies only when they violate cleanup regulations in the first place, while the protection goes to the public waters and communities that absorb spill damage. The main legitimate concerns are the severity of the per-day penalties for rule violations short of actual harm, and the reduced due-process protections for companies contesting penalty orders. On balance it is a targeted enforcement bill whose costs fall almost entirely on noncompliant operators.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Public Works and Transportation Committee, then to its Water Resources Subcommittee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ron Wyden of Oregon introduced the Oil Spill Disaster Prevention Act of 1990 in the House on May 23, 1990, joined by Reps. Les AuCoin and Michael DeFazio.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Public Works and Transportation on the day it was introduced.
On June 4, 1990, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Water Resources, and the action record shows no further activity — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action.
The bill attracted two cosponsors in the 257-member House Democratic majority and died in subcommittee when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Operators of oil and hazardous-substance facilities are better off, since they avoid the proposed fivefold-per-day penalty increase, mandatory compliance orders, and criminal exposure; the public gets no additional cleanup enforcement from this bill, though Congress pursued oil spill legislation more broadly in the wake of the same events.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken on the bill; its three named supporters were all Oregon Democrats and no member of either party is recorded as opposing it, so the partisan shape of any potential floor fight is unknown.

industries.industry: Oil shipping, storage, and petrochemical handlers
industries.note: The bill would have raised their cleanup-violation fines from $5,000 per violation to up to $25,000 per day per violation, added collection surcharges, mandatory compliance orders and audits, and criminal penalties for knowing or dangerous violations. Those costs fall only on firms that violate cleanup regulations, and they are the price of protecting public waters that absorb spill damage.
